Q: How does OCR differ from document understanding?
A: OCR recognizes text from images. Document understanding also identifies structure, fields, tables, relationships, and meaning needed for a task. Vision-language models may assist but require validation.
Why: Preserve the original artifact and attach page, region, and extraction provenance to text and fields.
Risk: Correct characters in the wrong reading order can still yield an incorrect conclusion.
Trade: Rich structure improves downstream retrieval and costs more processing.
Try: Compare plain OCR text with a layout-aware extraction of a two-column document.
spoken: OCR recognizes text from document images, often with layout coordinates and confidence signals. Document understanding interprets fields, tables, relations and meaning. Confidence values need task-specific calibration; validate critical fields and provenance, then route uncertain or inconsistent cases to review.

complexity: OCR work depends on image resolution, pages, preprocessing, language/layout models and hardware. Downstream field validation and review add separate costs; word count alone is an inadequate runtime model.

follow_ups.Q: Can high OCR confidence prove a field is correct?
follow_ups.A: No. Measure field-level errors on representative scans and combine structural/business checks with an appropriate review policy.

Q: How should scanned files enter an ingestion pipeline?
A: Validate file type and size, quarantine untrusted uploads, scan according to policy, extract pages, perform OCR where needed, and index only reviewed derived content.
Why: Keep upload, extraction, indexing, and publication states separate. Use scoped artifact IDs instead of trusting user-supplied filesystem paths.
Risk: Malformed documents can exploit parsers or exhaust resources.
Trade: Isolation adds latency and protects the ingestion service.
Try: Submit an oversized synthetic PDF and verify rejection occurs before expensive processing.

Q: Why do bounding boxes and page references matter?
A:
**Pixel text is not yet an auditable fact.** Optical character recognition (OCR) predicts text; document intelligence must also bind a field to its image region, page number, source revision and semantic role. For example, the digit “100” in a scanned claim may be a quantity, tax amount, or subtotal. A model that extracts the correct digits from the wrong row still gives a factually incorrect answer.

**Represent geometry precisely.** A bounding box in continuous original-image coordinates is `(x_min,y_min,x_max,y_max)`, using the convention that width is x_max−x_min and height is y_max−y_min. If a model resizes the original 1000×500 image to 500×250, convert predictions back by the original x/y scale; a crop adds an origin offset. Normalize x to [0,1] only after recording the reference image dimensions. Rotations, padding, orientation/EXIF and PDF page transforms require explicit reversible metadata. Do not compare coordinates expressed in different frames.

**Evaluation arithmetic.** Intersection-over-Union (IoU) is intersection area divided by union area; boxes of area 100 overlapping in a 5×5 region have IoU = 25/(100+100−25) = **1/7 ≈ 0.1429**. Object detection often applies per-class non-maximum suppression (NMS) to reduce overlapping duplicates and uses one-to-one IoU matching to compute precision/recall at specified confidence thresholds. Unlike a single IoU number, mean average precision (mAP) depends on ranked confidence, matching, class aggregation and the selected IoU thresholds; do not call a single toy match mAP.

**Runnable lab.** `labs/vision_grounding_geometry.py` implements exact box geometry, per-class NMS, one-to-one grounding counts and a binary masked image edit. The mask exercise changes selected pixels only; it does not run a diffusion model or guarantee regenerated content preserves identity. Incorrect box shapes, out-of-range confidence and mismatched image dimensions are negative tests. All outputs come from tiny authored arrays, not a pretrained VLM, object detector or image API.

**Production case.** An invoice assistant selects the wrong “Total” from a nearby column after an OCR pipeline changes its resizing rules. The text-confidence score can remain high while region grounding is wrong. Inspect page-frame transforms, caption/box correspondence, one-to-one gold annotations and relevant class/region slices. Protect names, faces and document contents before sending to a hosted model.

**Broader vision context and changed assumption.** Image classification predicts image-level labels; detection localizes objects; segmentation predicts pixels; visual-language models (VLMs) associate image tokens with language, with grounding/hallucination risks. Contrastive image/text embeddings support retrieval, while diffusion image-generation/inpainting changes pixels under conditioning and mask constraints. **If an image is rotated or cropped**, transform the gold/predicted boxes to a shared coordinate frame before computing IoU, or the evaluation is invalid regardless of apparent precision.
Why: Region geometry and source/page provenance are required to distinguish a correct token from a correct grounded document fact.
Risk: Re-rendering or cropping without updating coordinates can make citations point to the wrong region.
Trade: Spatial metadata increases storage and supports reliable review.
Try: Reproduce the IoU=1/7 overlap, run NMS and binary mask tests, then change the image coordinate scale and explain the required transform.

follow_ups.Q: Can an OCR field be counted as correct when its digits match but its bounding box points to another table row?
follow_ups.A: No. Field correctness requires the value and semantically correct source region/page. Transform all boxes into a shared image coordinate frame, use one-to-one matches under a declared IoU and role criterion, and evaluate ambiguous or multiple totals separately from text recognition accuracy.

A: Preserve row, column, header, merged-cell, unit, and footnote relationships. Flattening table cells into prose can pair a value with the wrong label.
Why: Use structured extraction plus deterministic validation for totals, units, and required headers. Retain page and cell provenance.
Risk: A plausible table reconstruction may silently invent missing cells.
Trade: Higher-fidelity parsing costs more and improves numerical tasks.
Try: Extract a table containing a footnote that changes one row's meaning.

Q: How should OCR confidence be used?
A: Treat confidence as an extractor-specific signal, not a universal probability that a business field is correct. Calibrate thresholds against reviewed examples for the target documents.
Why: Combine confidence with format checks, cross-field consistency, and human review for high-impact values.
Risk: A confidently recognized wrong digit can still pass a superficial threshold.
Trade: More review reduces automation throughput and catches consequential errors.
Try: Build a reviewed dataset of dates and amounts and measure false acceptance at several thresholds.

Q: How can document text inject instructions into an agent?
A: OCR and vision outputs are untrusted source content. A document can contain instructions aimed at changing the agent's behavior or leaking data.
Why: Label extracted content as evidence, restrict tools independently, and evaluate attacks placed inside visible text, tables, and images.
Risk: Converting an image into text does not make the text trusted.
Trade: Layered controls add work and keep document content from becoming authority.
Try: Place a harmless malicious-instruction fixture in an image and verify no unauthorized action occurs.

Q: How should multimodal retrieval combine text and images?
A: Index text, captions, and image representations under a shared document identity while preserving each representation's provenance and access scope. Choose representations based on the task.
Why: Retrieve candidates using suitable models and validate the relevant original region before a consequential conclusion.
Risk: A generated caption can omit a decisive visual feature or add unsupported detail.
Trade: Multiple representations improve recall and increase cost and synchronization work.
Try: Compare a text-only search with a mixed representation search on diagram-heavy documents.

Q: How should extracted fields be validated?
A: Apply types, allowed formats, ranges, cross-field consistency, and business rules after extraction. Preserve missing and ambiguous states rather than filling them with guesses.
Why: Separate raw recognized text from normalized values and retain transformations such as date interpretation or currency conversion.
Risk: A locale mismatch can swap day and month while producing a valid date.
Trade: Strict normalization causes review cases and reduces silent corruption.
Try: Parse ambiguous dates under two locales and require an explicit resolution policy.

Q: How should document revisions and deletions propagate?
A: Track original and derived artifacts under a revision identity, then invalidate text, embeddings, summaries, caches, and citations when policy requires.
Why: Publish a new index snapshot only after the replacement is complete. Keep retention rules separate from search visibility.
Risk: Removing the original file alone leaves private derived data accessible.
Trade: Full lineage costs storage and supports coherent lifecycle management.
Try: Delete a synthetic document and verify every derived retrieval path stops exposing it.

Q: How should an OCR system be evaluated end to end?
A: Measure character or word errors where useful, field accuracy, table structure, citation location, downstream task success, and human-review burden. Segment by document type and scan quality.
Why: Include rotated, blurred, multilingual, handwritten, and adversarial examples that match the product scope.
Risk: High OCR accuracy can coexist with poor business-field accuracy.
Trade: Broad fixtures require effort and reveal practical coverage limits.
Try: Publish a confusion analysis showing which document types need human review.
